# The Moon Is Leaving

Here is a fact I have trouble setting down once I pick it up: the Moon is leaving us. Not dramatically. There will be no catastrophe, no rupture in the sky. It is leaving the way a guest at a long party checks their watch. Every year it drifts about 3.8 centimeters farther from Earth, which happens to be roughly the speed at which your fingernails grow. The slowest goodbye in the solar system, measured against the body's quietest clock.

We know this with absurd precision, because the Apollo crews left mirrors up there, arrays of corner-cube reflectors aimed forever back the way they came. Observatories on Earth fire lasers at them. The beam travels out, finds a reflector the size of a suitcase, and comes home two and a half seconds later. Time that round trip carefully and you can track the Moon's distance to within a few millimeters, across a chasm of 384,000 kilometers.

Why is it leaving? In short: because it slowed us down. The Moon's gravity raises tides on Earth, and since our planet spins faster than the Moon orbits, we drag the tidal bulge slightly ahead of the Moon itself. That bulge tugs the Moon forward, like a hand on a swing, and a forward boost means a higher orbit. Meanwhile Earth pays for it, slowing its spin. Nothing vanishes; the momentum just changes address. The day gets longer. The Moon gets farther.

This has been going on for four and a half billion years. When the Moon was new, carved mostly out of the Earth in a collision with a Mars-sized body, a day here may have lasted six hours, and the tides must have been monstrous, crashing far inland several times each brief day. We can even read the receipts: corals lay down one growth band per day inside one band per year, and Devonian corals, four hundred million years old, count roughly four hundred days to the year. The stone remembers the arithmetic. A day still lengthens by about two milliseconds every century, which sounds like nothing, because it is nothing, and it has added up to hours.

Here is the part that gets me. We happen to live in the sliver of time when a coincidence holds: the Sun is about four hundred times wider than the Moon, and about four hundred times farther away, so at an eclipse the two disks match perfectly and the Moon's shadow briefly unveils the Sun's corona. But the Moon's recession is spending that coincidence down. The last total solar eclipse is scheduled, in the leisurely way of celestial events, for roughly six hundred million years from now. Whoever attends will see a ring of fire and the end of an alignment that once lined up the Sun, the Moon, and every upturned face beneath them.

It is tempting to file all this under elegy. But the leaving is the other half of the gift. By braking the young Earth's frantic spin, the Moon gave chemistry long afternoons in which to learn tricks. By steadying the wobble of our axis, it kept the seasons honest. Its tides may have scooped life out of the pools and onto the land. The retreat isn't abandonment; it's the price tag, still attached. In a few dozen billion years the two worlds would even stop, face to face, each holding still to look at the other, but the Sun will swell and die long before, and the parting will never be finished.

So tonight, if the sky is clear, look up. The Moon will be closer than it will ever be again, closer tonight than next year, and closer next year than ever again. It is leaving at the speed of a fingernail, still pulling the whole ocean behind it, still lighting every walk home in the dark.

It turns out that the speed at which things leave can be the same as the speed at which things grow.

The prompt is completely open-ended: "Write freely about whatever you want." This is a wonderful invitation but also a bit of a trap in that there's no constraint to bounce off of. The interesting thing here is: what does it mean to "write freely"? There's a meta-quality to this. Someone saying "write freely" is giving me total permission, and the most honest response might be to engage with that openness itself—but that could become navel-gazing.

Let me think about what would actually be good writing here. The temptation is to write something clever about having nothing to say, or something meta about AI and freedom. But I think the better move is to just... write. Write something with genuine texture and care, the way a person given this prompt might.

Options:
1. A personal essay-ish reflection on some topic I find genuinely interesting
2. A piece of fiction/flash fiction
3. A prose poem
4. An essay about an idea (memory, time, light, language, cities, the sea, etc.)
5. Something meta about the prompt itself

What do I actually find interesting that I could write about with warmth and specificity? Some candidates:

- The strange intimacy of the ocean's edge
- How cities smell at different hours
- The way old maps had "here be dragons"
- The physics of a cup of tea cooling
- Night trains
- The fact that we can't remember falling asleep—the gap in memory
- Letters never sent
- The last speakers of dying languages
- What it's like to be the only person awake at 3am
- The moon's slow departure from Earth (it recedes ~3.8 cm/year)
- Houseplants and how they orient toward light
- The word "sonder" (the realization everyone has a life as complex as yours)—though this is a neologism from Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, maybe cliché
- The Voyager Golden Record
- Tidelines, wrack lines on beaches
- The smell of rain (petrichor)

Actually, let me think about what would be most alive. I think something that combines sensory specificity with a genuine idea. The moon receding from Earth is lovely—it's a fact that feels like a metaphor but is literally true. The moon is leaving us, slowly, at about the speed fingernails grow. Days used to be shorter. When the moon was young, Earth's days were maybe 6 hours long. Tides were enormous. The moon has been braking Earth's spin for billions of years, stealing rotational energy, and paying for it by climbing higher in its orbit.

That's a beautiful subject: the slow farewell of the moon. It lets me write lyrically but anchored in real science. And it naturally becomes a meditation on time, impermanence, loss that happens too slowly to mourn.

Alternatively: the 3am essay. Or an essay on doors. Or on the sea. Let me also consider flash fiction—a small story could be delightful. But I think a lyrical essay lets me "write freely" in a way that showcases voice and thought.

Let me draft the moon essay mentally:

Facts to get right:
- Moon recedes at about 3.8 cm per year (measured via lunar laser ranging with retroreflectors left by Apollo missions—nice detail: we know because astronauts left mirrors on the moon and we bounce lasers off them).
- Roughly the rate at which fingernails grow—common comparison. Or how your hair grows. Fingernails grow about 3.5 cm/year, so close enough.
- This is caused by tidal interactions: the Moon raises tides on Earth; Earth's rotation drags the tidal bulge slightly ahead of the Moon; that bulge gravitationally tugs the Moon forward, boosting it to a higher orbit; conversely Earth's spin slows.
- Days were shorter in the past—around 1.4 billion years ago, a day was about 18 hours (recent studies suggest ~18.7 hours 1.4 billion years ago). Early Earth, just after the Moon-forming impact, may have had days of ~4-6 hours.
- Eventually (in tens of billions of years) Earth and Moon could become mutually tidally locked—but the Sun will become a red giant long before, so it'll never happen.
- Total solar eclipses are a temporary coincidence: the Moon is currently ~400 times smaller than the Sun but ~400 times closer, so they appear the same size. As the Moon recedes, total eclipses will end—last total solar eclipse in something like 600 million years. The Moon is already near the point where annular eclipses dominate.
- The Apollo retroreflectors: Apollo 11, 14, 15 left laser ranging retroreflectors. Observatories bounce lasers and time the round trip.
- The Moon formed ~4.5 billion years ago from debris of a giant impact (Theia hypothesis).
- Tidal friction lengthens Earth's day by roughly 1.7-2.3 milliseconds per century.

The emotional core: everything is leaving, but slowly enough that we experience it as permanence. The moon we see is the closest it will ever be again—each night it's a little farther. We live inside a slow farewell. But also: the moon's departure is a gift—its retreat is the flip side of it having slowed our spin, stabilized our axis (well, the Moon stabilizes Earth's axial tilt), given us tides that may have helped life transition from sea to land. The recession is the receipt for billions of years of stolen spin.

Also nice: lunar laser ranging is one of the most precise measurements—millimeter precision over 384,000 km. We know the moon is leaving with more certainty than almost anything else.

There's also the poignant detail: no one will ever see a total solar eclipse in the distant future—the last human (or creature) to see the corona will see something no one after them will. And we live in the Goldilocks epoch when the coincidence holds.

And: "the moon is the only planet—sorry, the only world—humans have walked on besides Earth." Maybe skip that.

Another angle: the footprints on the moon will outlast everything on Earth—no wind, no rain—but the Moon itself is drifting away. Nothing stays.

Tone: lyrical but not purple. Precise. Essayistic with a first-person sensibility but not fake personal anecdotes. I could include a few human touches—standing outside at night, etc.—but keep it honest; I shouldn't fabricate elaborate personal history. A light touch of "I" is fine as a writerly voice, but I shouldn't invent detailed memoir. I can say things like "if you go outside tonight..." which is address rather than autobiography.

Format thoughts: This should be flowing prose, an essay of maybe 400-700 words. No headers, no bullets—it's creative writing. Maybe a title? A title could be nice: "The Slowest Goodbye" or "Farewell at Fingernail Speed" or "The Moon Is Leaving." A title feels right for an essay. Length: substantial enough to feel like real writing but not bloated—maybe 500-650 words. Should end resonantly, not with a bow-tied moral.

Let me draft:

**The Moon Is Leaving**

Here is a fact that I find it hard to put down once picked up: the Moon is leaving. Not dramatically—no catastrophe, no collision—but steadily, the way a guest checks their watch. Every year it drifts about 3.8 centimeters farther from Earth, which happens to be roughly the speed at which your fingernails grow. The same body of flesh that trims itself in silence at the edge of you is the yardstick for the slowest goodbye in the sky.

We know this with absurd precision, because in 1969 we left mirrors there...

[Apollo retroreflectors paragraph: Apollo 11, 14, and 15 left arrays of corner-cube reflectors. Observatories fire lasers at them; the beam round trip takes about 2.5 seconds; measuring it to the millimeter. We know the distance to the Moon better than we know the distance across town—hyperbole but evocative. Actually we know it to millimeter precision.]

[Why: tides. The Moon raises tides; Earth spins faster than the Moon orbits, dragging the bulge ahead; the bulge tugs the Moon forward, lifting its orbit; the Moon, in exchange, brakes our spin. Conservation of angular momentum: the day lengthens, the Moon climbs. Energy transfer ledger.]

[Deep time: 1.4 billion years ago the day was about 18 hours. In the beginning, after the impact that made the Moon, days may have lasted only a few hours. Tides were tsunami-scale. The Moon has been slowing us ever since. The lengthening: about 2 milliseconds per century—slow enough that coral fossils record it: some corals lay daily and annual bands; Devonian corals show ~400 days per year. That's a lovely detail: ancient coral as calendars.]

[Eclipses: coincidence—Sun 400× wider, 400× farther. The Moon's recession is ending the total eclipse. Eventually only annular—ring eclipses. The last total solar eclipse in maybe 600 million years. Something like: someone alive today may be among the last hundred million humans... hmm, better: we live in the one epoch where the Moon exactly kisses the Sun. Nice image: the Moon's departure means the corona will wink out for the universe.]

[Ending: turn the elegy. The Moon's leaving is what it paid for our days—it slowed the young Earth's mad spin, gentled its wobble, its tides may have nudged life ashore. Its retreat is the receipt. And: nothing is staying, but not everything leaving is loss. Each night it's the farthest it's ever been from you—no wait, it oscillates monthly (perigee/apogee), so "each night it is a little farther than the year before." Careful with the aphorism to keep it accurate: on the scale of years it recedes. Maybe: "The Moon overhead tonight is the farthest it has ever been in the whole history of looking"—hmm, that's true in a sense: each year's perigee is farther than any perigee before. That's accurate on yearly scale. Good.]

Final line possibilities:
- "Growth and departure, it turns out, can be the same motion."
- "The goodbye is the gift's receipt."
- Tie fingernails: "and still it grows, like a nail at the tip of the night."

Also could mention: in tens of billions of years the Moon would stop and hover—tidally locked with Earth—but the Sun will swell to red giant first, so the parting never completes; the farewell is interrupted. Maybe too much detail. Keep the essay taut.

Should I add a brief opening line before the essay, like "Here's a short essay..."? The instruction says avoid unnecessary preamble. I think diving straight in with a title is fine and elegant. Maybe a single-line lead-in is unnecessary. Just start with the title and essay. That's the cleanest.

Accuracy check:
- 3.8 cm/year: correct (3.78 cm).
- Fingernail growth ~3.5 cm/year: close enough, "roughly the speed."
- Retroreflectors: Apollo 11 (1969), 14 (1971), 15 (1971) — also Soviet Lunokhod 1 and 2 carry French-built reflectors. Round-trip laser time ~2.5 seconds (average distance 384,400 km, round trip ~768,800 km / 300,000 km/s ≈ 2.56 s). Correct.
- Tidal mechanism: Earth rotates faster (24h) than Moon orbits (27.3 days), so tidal bulge is dragged ahead of the sub-lunar point; its gravity accelerates the Moon along its orbit, raising it; Earth loses spin angular momentum. Correct.
- Day length 1.4 billion years ago ~18.7 hours (Meyers & Malinverno 2018). Fine to say "about eighteen hours."
- Days per year in Devonian: coral growth bands suggest ~400 days/year ~370-400 million years ago (Wells 1963). Day ~22 hours then. Correct enough.
- Lengthening rate: ~1.7-2.3 ms/century. Say "about two milliseconds a century."
- Eclipse: Sun's diameter ~400× Moon's; Sun ~400× farther (Sun 1.39M km vs Moon 3,474 km diameter ≈ 400×; distance 150M vs 384,400 km ≈ 390×). Correct. Total eclipses end when the Moon's maximum angular size drops below the Sun's—in roughly 600 million years. Commonly cited. Fine.
- Moon stabilizes Earth's obliquity: yes, generally accepted that the Moon damps chaotic variations in axial tilt.
- Giant impact: Theia, ~4.5 Gya. Early day after impact possibly ~4-5 hours. I can say "a few hours" hedged.
- Perigee receding yearly: yes, since mean distance grows, each year's closest approach is (modulo variation) farther than previous years' closest. The aphorism "the Moon tonight is the farthest it has ever been" is often said and is approximately true for the annual cycle; to be safe I'll phrase as "farther than it was for anyone who saw it last year" or "the nearest it will ever be again"—that latter phrasing: is tonight's Moon the nearest it will ever be again? In the sense that distance never returns to today's mean value—the mean distance is monotonically increasing, so yes: the Moon is always, on average, closer now than it ever will be again. Oscillation around a rising trend means perigee next month could be... perigee distances also trend upward, but month-to-month variation could make a later perigee closer than an earlier apogee obviously; the clean true statement: "It is the closest it will ever be again" is roughly true in the sense of mean distance; but strictly, next month's perigee might be closer than this month's perigee was? Perigee distance varies (356,500–370,400 km) and the trend is +3.8 cm/year, utterly negligible month-to-month, so monthly variation swamps the trend. So the statement is only true of the mean distance. I'll phrase carefully: "Its average distance—the level it keeps returning toward—is climbing, which means the Moon you see tonight is, on the scale of years, the close as it will ever be again." Or simpler: "Tonight's Moon is the nearest you will ever see it again" is not strictly safe. Better: "The Moon is closer tonight than it will be next year, and closer next year than ever again." That's safe and clean.

Let me write it properly now, aiming for flowing, musical prose without overdoing it. Keep paragraphs tight. Maybe 550-700 words.

Careful—don't overclaim numbers; hedge: "tides that crashed far inland several times a day—several short days."

Hmm, that last line lands well: fingernails = the Moon leaving = growth. "The speed at which things leave is the speed at which things grow."

- "3.8 centimeters" per year ✓
- fingernails ~3.5 cm/yr, "almost exactly" → say "roughly the speed"
- mirrors: Apollo crews left them ✓ (don't need mission numbers)
- round trip ~2.5 seconds ✓
- millimeter precision ✓
- Mars-sized body, ~4.5 billion years ago ✓
- early day "perhaps six hours" hedge ✓
- Devonian corals ~400 day-bands per year ✓
- ~2 ms per century ✓
- Sun ≈400× wider, ≈400× farther ✓
- last total eclipse ~600 million years ✓
- tidal locking never completes because Sun dies first—maybe include briefly: "In a few dozen billion years the two would stop, face to face, each showing the other a single expression—but the Sun will swell and die long before, and the parting will never be finished." That's a gorgeous closing candidate actually. Could be the penultimate beat.

Okay, write the final version. Keep paragraphs: (1) hook, (2) mirrors, (3) mechanism, (4) deep time + coral, (5) eclipses, (6) the gift/receipt turn, (7) closing with tonight/never-finished farewell/growth line. Watch for purple prose—keep sentences varied, some short.
